oai_dc:dc.dc:description: <p>The growing process of violence in Mexico 2006 that is a result of the interpenetration of what we call “criminal order” and “legal order” in the construction of the drug trafficking monopoly, since at least 2006, tends to hide the historical process of selective extermination of social activists, including environmental activists. This article presents preliminary research results covering events of selective extermination recorded by press between January 2017 and April 2019. The objective of the paper is to make visible some characteristics of the process of violence that causes the gravest human costs – death, disappearance, or injuries, including torture and rape – suffered by those actors involved in struggles over water, land, forests or to prevent the construction of megaprojects, including mining, which affect the collective rights of their communities.</p>

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: <p><i>This issue of the WATERLAT-GOBACIT Network's Working Papers was organized</i></p><p><i>by members of the Network's Thematic Area 1, TA1 – X-disciplinarity in Research and</i></p><p><i>Action. TA1's membership includes academics, students, practitioners, representatives</i></p><p><i>of social movements and civil society organizations, among others. This TA has a</i></p><p><i>crosscutting function with interlinkages with the other Thematic Areas, of the Network,</i></p><p><i>as it focuses on theoretical and methodological aspects concerning the challenges and</i></p><p><i>opportunities facing our endeavours to produce knowledge about water from inter- and</i></p><p><i>trandisciplinary perspectives.</i></p><p><i>This particular issue offers significant contibutions that are relevant to all TA's but</i></p><p><i>some articles also address specific empirical examples that are connected with topics</i></p><p><i>covered by TA2 – Water and Megaprojects , TA3–, Urban Water Cycle and Essential Public</i></p><p><i>Services, TA6–Hydrosocial Basins, Territories, and Spaces,TA7– Art, Communication,</i></p><p><i>Culture, and Education, and TA8– Water-related Disasters. The issue features five articles, three in Spanish and the remaining two in English and</i></p><p><i>Portuguese, respectively.</i></p><p><i>Article 1, by Enrique Luengo González, addresses the challenges and obstacles</i></p><p><i>facing scientific institutions, particularly universities, to generate the conditions</i></p><p><i>required for developing, producing, and circulating knowledge that, beyond rhetorical</i></p><p><i>arguments and formal statements, actually embraces inter-and transdisciplinary</i></p><p><i>approaches. Among other issues, the author discusses the lack of institutional and</i></p><p><i>financial resources required for the promotion and strentghtening of these approaches</i></p><p><i>that seek to trascend monodisciplinary enclosures.The article explores the difficulties</i></p><p><i>facing universities to organize and sustain over time research teams dedicated to the</i></p><p><i>development of collective forms of knowledge informed by these approaches and</i></p><p><i>oriented at solving complex problems, involving a wide range of actors beyond the</i></p><p><i>academic sphere. Some of the obstacles identified are the lack of resources to support</i></p><p><i>the processes of mediation and negotiation to generate adequate conditions for the</i></p><p><i>production and dissemination of this type of knowledge, which is needed to provide</i></p><p><i>collective solutions to complex problems, including proposals for practical action. The</i></p><p><i>author argues that there is an urgent need to strengthen the capacities of universities </i></p><p><i>to develop more situated, multidimensional, and complex approaches, and reorganize</i></p><p><i>their teaching and research structures to improve their ability to contribute towards the</i></p><p><i>development of more hopeful futures for human communities, particularly for the more</i></p><p><i>vulnerable sectors. The final comments highlight some promising examples suggesting</i></p><p><i>that inter-and transdisciplinary approaches have a fundamental role to play in the</i></p><p><i>contributions that universities can make in providing support for solving the highly</i></p><p><i>complex problems facing humakind in this historical stage. In Article 2, Norma Georgina Gutierrez Serrano discusses the design and</i></p><p><i>implementation of transdisciplinary research methods in the context of networks and</i></p><p><i>groups of researchers in Mexico. The author grounds the arguments in her experience</i></p><p><i>working closely with these research networks and groups which included following</i></p><p><i>up, and, occasionally participating in their activities. The article gives attention to</i></p><p><i>the diversity of forms and dynamics of the transdisciplinarity in research activities</i></p><p><i>practiced by these actors, and draws lessons about the interrelations that have allowed</i></p><p><i>these networks and groups to succeed in establishing the ground for transdiciplinary</i></p><p><i>research and also discussses how their practices also nurture the emergence of new</i></p><p><i>interrelations, thus contributing to the reproduction and expansion of transdisciplinary</i></p><p><i>approaches even in environments that not necessarily give priority or fully support these</i></p><p><i>initiatives. The author emphasises that a key principle in the creation and development</i></p><p><i>of transdisciplinary research activities is "thinking and acting with care", whereby</i></p><p><i>interrelations between researchers and other actors are characterized by the presence</i></p><p><i>of affective forms of human relations. In her view, transdisciplinary research is a "form</i></p><p><i>of producing commons".  Article 3, by Norma Valencio, addresses the contradictions and obstacles facing</i></p><p><i>research initiatives that seek to "trespass" monodisciplinary enclosures often fiercely</i></p><p><i>defended by institutional barriers, material interests and other hurdles. The author</i></p><p><i>draws her reflections from experiences characterizing the production of scientific</i></p><p><i>knowledge in the post-Dictatorship context of Brazil since the 1980s. She argues</i></p><p><i>that during this period, scientific institutions increasingly faced the demands of social</i></p><p><i>movements and other social actors affected by a wide array of socio-environmental</i></p><p><i>crises and conflicts. The article examines some research initiatives that provide a model</i></p><p><i>of commitment towards supporting grassroots struggles against socio-environmental</i></p><p><i>injustice and inequality by developing inter-and transdisciplinary approaches and</i></p><p><i>practices. Although the pioneering examples discussed are a source of encouragement,</i></p><p><i>the author highlights the fact that some of the more difficult challenges and obstacles</i></p><p><i>faced by these initiatives come from entrenched traditions of "disciplinary purism" and</i></p><p><i>the institutional organization of the scientific system itself. Article 4, was co-authored by Gisela Ariana Rausch, Rosa Paola Aviña Escot, Lorena</i></p><p><i>Bottaro, Ana Nuñez, Franco Salvadores, Marian Sola Alvarez, and Laura PriscilaTercero</i></p><p><i>Cruz. The paper is a product of a Research Workshop focused on the propositions put</i></p><p><i>forward by Christian Laval and Pierre Dardot on the concept of "common". The workshop</i></p><p><i>included a Dialogue with Pierre Dardot that took place in one of the sessions. The</i></p><p><i>authors discuss the implications and applicability of Laval and Dardot's understanding</i></p><p><i>of "the common" for inter-and transdisciplinary research initiatives focused on social</i></p><p><i>grievances and conflicts connected with water-related environmental injustices and inequalities in Latin America. The discussion presented draws from research carried</i></p><p><i>out by the authors in Argentina, Guatemala, and Mexico. The article argues that Laval</i></p><p><i>and Dardot's conceptualization of the "common" proposes a resignification of this</i></p><p><i>concept and an invitation to wider disciplinary diversity in addressing the topic, which is</i></p><p><i>required to develop more adequate conceptual frameworks to account for the growing</i></p><p><i>complexity of socio-environmental processes. In Article 5, Luciano Villalba and Bianca Vienni-Baptista present an assesment</i></p><p><i>of the implementation of a water-related transdisciplinary research and intervention</i></p><p><i>project involving university researchers, public institutions and civil society actors</i></p><p><i>in the City of Tandil, Province of Buenos Aires, Argentina. The authors' analysis is</i></p><p><i>informed by the heuristic Transdisciplinary Framework developed under the leadership</i></p><p><i>of Vienni-Baptista. The article presents details of this methodological framework for</i></p><p><i>transdisciplinary research and shows how it provides a useful tool for the design,</i></p><p><i>implementation, and evaluation of inter-and transdisciplinary projects.The paper places</i></p><p><i>emphasis on the complexities of processes of knowledge production oriented by</i></p><p><i>inter-and transdisciplinary approaches and casts light on the significance of learning</i></p><p><i>from unsuscessful activities, which often provide key information for tuning and</i></p><p><i>improving the design and implementation of research projects. In the particular case</i></p><p><i>examined by the authors, factors like the wider political context, the level of commitment</i></p><p><i>from key participants, failures of communication between different hierarchic levels of</i></p><p><i>the project's organizational structure, and the obstacles faced to achieve a meaningful</i></p><p><i>involvement of citizens and community representatives, particularly women, were</i></p><p><i>identified as important reasons for the eventual weakening and stagnation of the project.</i></p>

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: <p>After reviewing some relevant elements of the trajectory and conjuncture of extractive activities in Chile, derived from the institutional architecture for the commodification and privatization of water articulated around the 1981 Water Code and the 1980 Political Constitution, the paper describes the communicational, political and socioenvironmental controversy developed in the Copiapo Valley, Atacama Region. The article looks at the communicational deployment made by sectors of the social groups that own the water market linked to agriculture, who have sought to position their own interests around their Lautaro 2.0 Project. The paper identifies the actors involved as well as the contestation strategies from civil society sectors, showing how the institutional frameworks that guarantee the water property system emerge as one of the nodal elements in the discursive networks that subvert and reveal the interests of the property-owning sectors.</p>
